text: This F1 car is running its biggest wing, and it barely grips.
This weekend, F1 races in Mexico City 2,240 meters up, the highest track on the calendar.
Up here, the air is nearly a quarter thinner.
Less air means less push on the wing.
So teams bolt on their biggest, Monaco-style wings,
and still get about as much downforce as Monza's skinny ones.
I'm doing everything right. Thin air hits the engine too. The turbo spins up to 15%
faster just to breathe. And with so little air, cooling the brakes and engine is hard.
So bigger vents everywhere. But here's the twist. Thin air also means less drag.
On the long straight here, in 2016,
Valteri Bottas hit 372.5 kilometers an hour,
the fastest speed ever recorded in an F1 race.
Maximum wing, maximum speed, only in Mexico.
Thin air? I call it a cheat code.
